source: Danek & Flanagin (2019) Cognitive conflict and restructuring: the neural basis of two core components of insight
finding: Defines cognitive conflict as detecting information that does not fit the current mental representation. It is not response conflict (Stroop). If the conflict cannot be resolved the solver is at an impasse. Restructuring is the second step. Conflict is a prerequisite for restructuring (after Luo and Knoblich).
numbers: Design: fMRI, 20 magic-trick videos (6.3 to 42.5 s). Incongruent cue (new, contradicting information) versus congruent cue (repeats the false view). Contrast incongruent > congruent = conflict; correct > incorrect solution = restructuring.
quote: Cognitive conflict ... must be differentiated from response conflict where a decision has to be made between several competing actions
limits: Conflict and restructuring are inferred from cue type and solution accuracy, not measured directly. Aha ratings were deliberately not collected because cues alter them.
agent_relevance: Gives a two-step model for S6: (1) detect the clash, (2) change the representation. Our detector should fire on the clash, not on time spent.

source: Danek & Flanagin (2019) Cognitive conflict and restructuring: the neural basis of two core components of insight
finding: Cue manipulation worked. Helpful incongruent cues raised solution rates from 26% to 59%. The helpful cue was also rated more helpful.
numbers: N=30 analysed after two exclusions (they already knew 17 and 16 of 20 tricks). 572 valid observations (285 incongruent, 287 congruent). Solution rate 0.59 (SD 0.49) vs 0.26 (SD 0.44), F(1,570)=58.81, p<.001, d=0.64. Helpfulness 0.72 vs 0.26, F=107.33, d=0.87. Overall 42.3% correct, 28.7% wrong, 29.0% no answer. Spontaneous solving after one viewing was below 13% (mean 2.9%).
limits: The cue is applied after viewing, so it is a hint that contradicts the false view, not an organic conflict. Solved tricks per person ranged 3 to 12. Condition ratio was 9:11 by a seeding error.
agent_relevance: A hint that contradicts the working assumption gave about 2.3x the solve rate of a hint that agrees with it. In our agent, an error message that names the clashing assumption should beat a generic retry.

source: Danek & Flanagin (2019) Cognitive conflict and restructuring: the neural basis of two core components of insight
finding: Conflict (incongruent > congruent cue) activated posterior, mostly visual areas, thalamus, hippocampus, temporal lobes, frontal eye fields and some frontal cortex. The reverse contrast showed nothing. The authors read this as prediction error plus attention to the cue-relevant sensory domain plus default-mode state.
numbers: Threshold p<.001 voxel-wise, p<.05 FWE cluster-corrected. Angular gyrus and middle temporal gyrus were active in both conflict and restructuring.
limits: Reverse inference from brain regions to cognitive processes is weak. Single lab, single paradigm (magic tricks). Visual material may drive the posterior pattern.
agent_relevance: Conflict looks like a prediction-error signal, so a program that compares output to an expected result is a fair analogue.

source: Danek & Flanagin (2019) Cognitive conflict and restructuring: the neural basis of two core components of insight
finding: Restructuring (correct > incorrect solutions) engaged a wide network: default mode, executive control and salience networks. Left inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis) was among the clusters.
numbers: Example clusters: L IFG pars triangularis 356 voxels, p(FWE)=0.008. R angular gyrus 266 voxels, p=0.026.
limits: Correct vs incorrect solution is a coarse proxy for restructuring. Participants solved after the cue, so cue effect and solution effect overlap.
agent_relevance: Restructuring is not one local operation. It recruits control and memory systems together, which fits a scaffold that hands the model a full re-read of the problem rather than a patch.

source: Danek & Flanagin (2019) Cognitive conflict and restructuring: the neural basis of two core components of insight
finding: Prior insight fMRI is inconsistent. Dietrich and Kanso found ACC most often and no support for right-hemisphere dominance. The Sprugnoli meta-analysis also found no right-brain dominance and many scattered regions. The authors blame mixed operationalisations of insight (cues, shown solutions, choices, Aha ratings).
numbers: Sprugnoli list (left): precentral gyrus, middle temporal gyrus, precuneus, cingulate, claustrum, middle occipital gyrus, uvula, insula. Right: superior frontal gyrus, insula, precuneus, middle temporal gyrus.
limits: These are the Danek paper's summaries; the original meta-analyses were not opened.
agent_relevance: Neural localisation is not a reliable basis for design. Use behavioural signatures (stalls, repeated moves) instead.

source: Luo and Knoblich (2007), as cited in Danek & Flanagin (2019)
finding: Luo and Knoblich proposed that cognitive conflict is needed to trigger a change of problem representation. Restructuring is the essential feature of insight problem solving.
numbers: Quoted via Danek & Flanagin only.
limits: Not opened. Treat as a relayed claim.
agent_relevance: Supports using detected conflict as the trigger for a reframing step (S6) and not reframing on a schedule (G1).

source: Danek & Flanagin (2019), relayed claims about earlier work
finding: Earlier work reports all-or-none solving (no partial solution information before the solution), that people cannot predict success on insight problems (Metcalfe), and that warmth ratings do not track progress. Pilot cues in magic-trick work roughly doubled solution rates, and pictorial cues beat verbal cues.
numbers: Relayed from the introduction and methods, with citations to Danek and colleagues.
limits: Not opened at source. The all-or-none claim is contested by Fedor 2015 (recurring search and impasse).
agent_relevance: An agent cannot trust its own sense of progress. Progress must be counted by code.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Founding test of representational change theory (Ohlsson 1992). Matchstick arithmetic problems vary the scope of the constraint that must be relaxed (Type A narrow, B wider, C widest) and the tightness of the chunk to be decomposed (Type D, V or X into sticks). Predicted difficulty C < B < A and A < D was found.
numbers: Exp 1A, N=20, German students, 5 min limit, 6 problems per block. Median solution time Block 1: A 40 s, B 155 s, C 300 s (time limit), D 140 s. Frequency main effect of type F(3,57)=7.11, p<.001. Type D: 75% solved in Block 1 vs 90% in Block 2, transfer ns (p=.13).
quote: the differences were C < B < A and A < D
limits: Small samples. Matchstick arithmetic is narrow and well structured. Exp 2 (US students) gave the same ordering; its N was not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Difficulty is set by how wide a hidden assumption is, and by how tightly the input is bound into units. A reframing step should list the assumptions in play and relax the narrowest first.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Strong one-shot transfer. One exposure to a hard type made it as easy as Type A. Type A showed no transfer because it was already easy.
numbers: Interaction type x block F(3,57)=3.24, p<.05. Transfer significant for B (p<.05) and C (p<.001), not for A (p=.80). Solution-time transfer: B p<.001, C p<.01, D p<.05 (Wilcoxon).
limits: Transfer within one session and one format. No delayed test.
agent_relevance: After one successful relaxation, store the same relaxation and offer it first on similar tasks (a learned move, not a reasoned one).

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Experiment 3 tested constraint relaxation directly. A tautology form (e.g. III = III = III) is only possible when the 'equations must not be tautologies' constraint is dropped. Seeing tautological problems first made later regular Type C problems easy, but did not help Type D (chunk decomposition).
numbers: Exp 3, N=34. Regular-first group solved only 61% of Type C in Block 1. Tautological Type C items were all solved in Block 1. Block 2 solve rates 92% vs 94%. Block 1 group difference chi2(1,N=34)=12.59, p<.001. Block 1 regular vs Block 2 tautology-first: Type C U=8, Z=4.67, p<.001; Type D U=65, Z=2.71, p<.01; Type A ns.
limits: Shows that being told a form is valid is enough to drop a constraint. It does not show what solvers drop spontaneously.
agent_relevance: Telling a model that a normally forbidden move is allowed can unlock a solution. A scaffold can pass an explicit list of constraints that may be relaxed.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Two separate sources of difficulty: constraint scope and chunk tightness. Type D was about as hard as Type B. The authors say relaxation need not be deliberate.
numbers: Type D vs A: Wilcoxon on Block 1 solution times T=10, p<.001, N=20. A vs B T=12, p<.001. B vs C T=41, p<.05.
limits: Rival account: Kaplan & Simon (1990), see a12. These data do not fully separate the accounts.
agent_relevance: Two repair moves, not one: loosen a rule, and break a unit apart (re-tokenise the input).

source: Kaplan & Simon (1990), as described in Knoblich et al. (2001) and a web search summary
finding: Rival account. Impasses arise because the first representation is incomplete, not because it is misleading. Solvers escape by encoding more features. Ohlsson holds that insight problems actively mislead.
numbers: No new numbers. Cited as the competing explanation.
limits: Not opened at source. Knoblich 2001 lists it with the fixedness and ruts accounts.
agent_relevance: For an LLM both can occur: a missing fact versus a wrong frame. The agent should test both repairs.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Eye movements support the claim that impasse follows a misleading initial representation. Fixation duration rises over time on the hard problems (impasse), and attention is biased to numerals before the operator constraint is relaxed.
numbers: N=24, 1000 Hz oculometer, 3 matchstick problems, 5 min limit. Solved: Problem A (change result value) 23/24; Problem C (tight chunk) 18/24; Problem B (change operator) 9/24; B vs A chi2(1,24)=18.38, p<.001; C vs A chi2=4.18, p<.05; B vs C chi2=4.78, p<.05. Mean fixation duration: problem effect F(2,44)=3.49, p<.05 (B and C > A); interval effect F(2,44)=8.58, p<.001; interaction ns.
limits: Mean fixation duration did not differ between solvers and non-solvers. Small N. Solvers did attend more to the crucial chunk in the first two intervals, F(1,22)=7.09, p<.05.
agent_relevance: Impasse has a behavioural signature: slower, longer looks with no new moves. A code monitor can look for repeated or stalled output as the impasse signal.

source: Fedor, Szathmary & Ollinger (2015) Problem solving stages in the five square problem
finding: Tests the classic four-stage model (search, impasse, insight, search) with behaviour, not self-report. Impasse was defined from behaviour as inactivity or repeated moves. Most people did not follow the classic order. Search and impasse recurred several times.
numbers: N=129 after exclusions, 101 analysed (34 control with 15 solvers, 67 impasse-monitoring with 24 solvers). Solution rate 39%. Classic order: 19/39 solvers (49%) and 8/62 non-solvers (13%). Recurring search and impasse: 20 solvers (51%) and 53 non-solvers.
quote: the majority of participants did not follow the classic four-stage model of insight
limits: Online crowd sample (CrowdFlower level 3). 28 participants excluded, 26 of whom solved in under 32 s (likely knew it). Impasse defined from behaviour by the authors.
agent_relevance: Impasse is not one event followed by a single reframe. Expect loops. The detector must be able to fire more than once and the budget must allow it.

source: Fedor, Szathmary & Ollinger (2015) Problem solving stages in the five square problem
finding: Self-reports of impasse are unreliable. Non-solvers reported impasse more than solvers, but people did not report impasse more often during behaviourally defined impasse stages. Insight reports match solving.
numbers: 74% of solvers (29/39) vs 10% of non-solvers (6/62) reported insight; chi2(1,N=101)=41.42, p<.0001, phi=.64.
limits: Button reporting may disturb the task, hence the control group.
agent_relevance: Do not ask the model whether it is stuck. Detect it from output. This fits G1 (doubt only on a signal that code can check).

source: Schonauer et al. (2018) Sleep does not promote solving classical insight problems and magic tricks
finding: Failed to find the claimed benefit of incubation or sleep for restructuring. Neither raised solution rates or insight-type solutions in magic tricks and classic insight problems.
numbers: N=77. Retest solved 1.40 +/- 0.13 extra magic tricks. Incubation F(1,64)=0.008, p=.930; sleep state F(1,64)=0.047, p=.829. Initial phase 2.66 +/- 0.21 tricks. 54 +/- 6.3% of solutions had insight. REM (n=7) 20.6% vs no REM (n=9) 19.8%, t(14)=0.091, p=.929.
limits: Daytime nap design, 3 h gap. Insight-only analysis numerically favoured incubation (F(1,46)=2.305, p=.136, partial eta2=.048) but was not significant. Cai et al. (2009) found a REM benefit on the RAT.
agent_relevance: Pausing alone does not resolve an impasse. A restart without a changed frame or new information should not be expected to help.

source: Hedne, Norman & Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks
finding: Self-labelled insight solutions are more accurate and more confident, but warmth ratings did not differ between insight and non-insight solutions. This does not match the Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) pattern.
numbers: N=51, 32 magic-trick videos of 15 s. 971 trials analysed after excluding 661. 29% reported solved with insight, 71% not. Inter-rater alpha=0.911. Confidence tracked accuracy more for non-insight than insight trials. After insight solutions, people were more likely to repeat their wrong answers on a later recognition test.
limits: Only trials with 3 or 4 warmth ratings were used, which excluded about 70% of trials. The original study allowed up to 40 ratings. Magic tricks may mix insight and incremental routes.
agent_relevance: A sudden, confident solution can be a wrong one that sticks. A confident reframing must still be checked against held-out evidence (G3).

source: Ollinger, Fedor, Brodt & Szathmary (2017) Insight into the ten-penny problem: guiding search by constraints and maximization
finding: Relaxing constraints is necessary but not sufficient. Hints to use lines and intersections only worked when a search criterion (maximise intersections per line) was also given. Solvers made promising moves earlier and varied attempts more.
numbers: N=120 in four groups of 30 (control, lines, intersections, maximization). Logistic regression: maximization after 5 min OR 2.18 (95% CI 1.04 to 4.57, p=.04), variation after 5 min OR 3.99 (CI 1.33 to 12.00, p=.01); model chi2(6,115)=63.51, Nagelkerke R2=.61, 87.8% classified. 28% of the maximization group still failed.
limits: One puzzle. The prediction of near-100% success in the maximization group failed: either another source of difficulty or working-memory overload.
agent_relevance: Reframing alone does not finish the job. After relaxing, the scaffold must give a score to search against and force variation across attempts instead of repeating one.

source: Tik et al. (2018) Ultra-high-field fMRI insights on insight: neural correlates of the Aha! moment
finding: 7 T fMRI during a German remote-associates task shows that an insightful solution engages subcortical reward regions (thalamus, hippocampus, VTA, nucleus accumbens, caudate) as well as left anterior middle temporal gyrus. The authors argue the affective part of Aha is dopaminergic.
numbers: N=29 analysed (30 recruited, 1 excluded). Age 27.7 +/- 3.7. Online norming sample of 163 for the German RAT.
limits: This studies the reward at the moment of solution, not the earlier conflict. RAT is a verbal association task, not a representation clash.
agent_relevance: The reward at solution is not available to an LLM. A code-checked pass must stand in for that signal.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive chameleon or stubborn sloth: revealing the behavior of large language models in knowledge conflicts
finding: Direct LLM test of conflict between internal belief and new evidence. When the contradicting passage is coherent and LLM-generated, models are highly receptive. When it is built by word substitution (incoherent), models stick to memory, and larger models in a family stick more.
numbers: Eight LLMs including ChatGPT, GPT-4, PaLM2, Qwen-7B, Llama2-7B and 70B, Vicuna-7B and 33B. Final example counts per model range from 500 to 1,356 in the conflict subset. Answer-inconsistency rate on the elicitation check ranged 0.7% to 16.6%.
limits: ICLR 2024. Counter-memory is LLM-generated, so its fluency may favour acceptance. QA facts, not problem solving.
agent_relevance: A clash has to be shown in coherent form with an explicit contradicting statement to move a model. A bare failing output may not be enough; the scaffold should phrase the conflict clearly.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive chameleon or stubborn sloth: revealing the behavior of large language models in knowledge conflicts
finding: Confirmation bias. When both supporting and conflicting evidence are present, models prefer evidence that matches their own memory. The bias grows with the amount of memory-consistent evidence and for popular entities. GPT-4 had an 80% memorisation ratio on the most popular questions. Models also follow evidence order and the majority of evidence.
numbers: GPT-4 and Vicuna-33B still clung to memory when the counter-answer had more evidence (ratio 1/3). Evidence order changed answers by over 5% for several models and over 30% for PaLM2 and Llama2-7B. StrategyQA integration test: models failed to integrate evidence correctly in 38.2% of examples.
limits: Zero-shot, no scaffold. The memorisation ratio measures answer choice, not insight.
agent_relevance: Models resist information that clashes with their first view. A clash signal has to be adjudicated by code (tests, retrieval), not by the model's own preference (G5).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: LLMs cannot use their own sense of conflict to repair reasoning. Without an oracle label, asking a model to review and revise lowers accuracy. With oracle labels gains are large, but those gains rely on knowing the answer is wrong.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic self-correction, 1 / 3 / 5 calls: GSM8K 75.9 / 75.1 / 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 / 38.1 / 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 / 25.0 / 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 / 91.5 / 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 / 79.5 / 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 / 49.0 / 43.0. Oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0. GPT-3.5 kept its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: ICLR 2024. Prompts from earlier papers. Newer reasoning models are not covered. Table layout in the extracted PDF is ambiguous, so recheck rows before quoting.
agent_relevance: Evidence for G1 and G2: the conflict trigger must be external (a failed check), because model-sensed conflict can hurt.

source: Xu et al. (2024) Knowledge conflicts for LLMs: a survey
finding: Survey sorts conflicts into three types: context-memory, inter-context and intra-memory. It reviews causes, model behaviour and solutions, split into pre-hoc and post-hoc fixes. Context-memory conflict is the most studied. It notes confirmation bias in LLMs: models favour the context that matches their prior.
numbers: Taxonomy in Figure 3 and a dataset table (Table 1) list evaluation sets by conflict type.
limits: Survey. Only the structure and introduction were read in detail, not each cited study.
agent_relevance: The agent faces all three: prompt vs memory, two tool outputs that disagree, and its own inconsistent answers. Handle each in code (retrieve, run, compare).

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The metacognitive bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal fundamental limits of machine insight and self-evaluation in reasoning AI (NazoNazo)
finding: Benchmark of insight-like Japanese children's riddles that need representational restructuring. Models are far below humans on the same subset. Models often write the right answer in their thought log and then do not choose it (verification failure).
numbers: 201 riddles, human reference on 120 items (n=126, mean 52.9%). 38 frontier LLMs, retrieval-free, zero-shot: non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%. GPT-5 was the outlier, within the human 95% CI. Verification failures were 5.23% (Gemini 2.5) to 39.34% (Grok-4) of wrong answers; Claude Opus 4 25.00%. Pooled odds ratio 2.29 on the full 201 items.
limits: Thought-log analysis needs the gold answer to appear verbatim. Only models with usable logs were counted. Small Japanese human sample. Authors call the false-insight link a descriptive analogy.
agent_relevance: Generation is not the main gap; commitment is. A scaffold should keep every candidate the model produces and have code, not the model, pick one with a held-out test.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The metacognitive bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal fundamental limits of machine insight and self-evaluation in reasoning AI (NazoNazo)
finding: Thought logs also show 'false insight': the model settles with apparent confidence on a wrong reinterpretation. The authors link this to false Aha in humans (Danek & Wiley 2017).
numbers: Descriptive only. No prevalence rate given.
limits: Qualitative, not a measured rate.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as Hedne 2016: confident reframings need an outside check before they are kept.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a mental set?
finding: Tests set effects on three LLMs with the mathematical-equivalence task of DeCaro (2016): complex-first vs shortcut-first order. Chain-of-thought lifted accuracy but made models use more steps, which the authors read as a mental-set shift. Examples did not change step count.
numbers: Models: Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, GPT-4o. 12 problems (6 complex, 6 shortcut). Llama-3.1-8B shortcut problems exact match 0.16 under few-shot. Llama-3.1-70B and GPT-4o did better on complex than shortcut problems under few-shot plus CoT.
limits: Very small problem set, three models, no significance tests seen. An analogy to mental set rather than a test of impasse.
agent_relevance: Weak. Do not rely on set effects as an LLM trigger without a stronger study.

source: Wiley & Danek (2024), cited in Mizumoto et al. (2025)
finding: Cited as the current review of insight problem solving: insight progresses through impasse and restructuring, with monitoring and control shaping performance.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Only the citation context was read.
agent_relevance: Pointer for the next round of reading.

source: Ohlsson (1992) Information-processing explanations of insight and related phenomena, via a web search summary and Knoblich et al. (1999)
finding: Representational change theory. Impasse arises when search under a misleading representation runs out. Three mechanisms can break it: constraint relaxation, re-encoding and elaboration. Knoblich 1999 added chunk decomposition.
numbers: Mechanisms only; no data.
limits: Chapter not opened; secondary summary only.
agent_relevance: Direct template for O6 (reframe): relax a constraint, re-encode, or add information.
